# Task 1 — Critique of a Manipulative Visualization

```{=latex}
\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{0.52\textwidth}
\vspace{0pt}\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.82\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../data/task_01/bad_example.jpeg}\\[0.5em]
{\footnotesize\color{darkstone}\itshape Source: White House (2026)}
\end{minipage}\hfill\begin{minipage}[t]{0.44\textwidth}
\vspace{0pt}
```

*The most obvious issue is the truncated y-axis, which exaggerates the perceived change in steel production and creates an immense lie factor. On top of overstating the change, the chart also uses color encoding to further mislead the viewer. They make the fill of the prior year red and that of 2025 green, which in western societies conveys positive sentiment. They also add a green font to the "INCREASES" to really convey a positive development. They additionally cherry-pick a two-year comparison, which is not representative of the historical range of US steel production. Two data points are not enough to tell a story. A minor issue I don't like either is the naming of the x-axis, where in one instance the year is at the start and in another at the end.*

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}
```

# Task 3 — Critique of a Particularly Good Visualization

```{=latex}
\noindent\begin{minipage}[t]{0.52\textwidth}
\vspace{0pt}\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.82\textheight,keepaspectratio]{../data/task_03/rare_earths_di.png}\\[0.5em]
{\footnotesize\color{darkstone}\itshape Source: Our World in Data (2026)}
\end{minipage}\hfill\begin{minipage}[t]{0.44\textwidth}
\vspace{0pt}
```

*This is a good visualization because it tells a clear story. This story is supported by the fact that the maker chose to sort the reserves by descending order, making the disparity between reserves and production immediately apparent. The chart uses color, but in a good way that makes the distinction between the two variables easy to see. The axis is not truncated and the bars lengths faithfully represent the data.*

*There are some minor issues worth mentioning though. The visualization uses "selected countries" for the visualization, which leaves me to question what criteria determined which countries were included. The graph also shows percentages <0.1% which then are not truthful to the size of the bars. Finally, they include a measure of a country that does not have recorded reserves. This makes it questionable whether this is a valid data point.*

```{=latex}
\end{minipage}
```

# Task 15 --- Favorite Classical (Non-AI) Data-Viz Tools

- **R** --- R is probably the base of my favorite classical non-AI data visualization tools. I like R because it is the first programming language that I learned, and also because the data visualizations in R look very nice. While I do prefer Python for a lot of different use cases, and even prefer it over R in most cases, I believe that R is the best for data visualization specifically given its library ggplot2, which I will discuss in the next bullet.
- **ggplot2** --- As mentioned above, ggplot2 is probably my favorite library for data visualizations, especially static ones. The output looks very clean and professional, and I feel like it's what most professionals use in the industry. What I like about it is how you build the visualization up by levels, and it makes intuitive sense to me the way it is built up. I don't like Matplotlib. It looks more childish, so to speak, and it's less intuitive in my eyes.
- **`design_system.R`** --- This is not necessarily a tool in the sense that the others are, but it is something that I created myself. It is a document that outlines what I would like in my data visualizations. Here I specified the colors, the font, and everything I want in terms of visualization, and Claude would always refer to this and use it as the base for its design of visualizations, in order to ensure that the visualizations have a common theme and it doesn't start drifting around or changing colors slightly or using different fonts.
- **Quarto** --- Quarto is the tool that I use to create this portfolio. I recently stumbled upon it in our Introduction to Programming course that I took this semester. I like the way that I can put everything into Quarto, and it uses LaTeX to then render the portfolio. It creates one unified document that I can have everything inside of, and that renders nicely into the portfolio.
- **VS Code** --- VS Code is the classic IDE for coding, and it is also what I've been using now. I've heard that Cursor has better AI integration, but I've used VS Code in the past and I feel comfortable with how it works. I feel like the AI integration in VS Code is already good enough. The only drawback of VS Code is that it's not as good for R, but nevertheless it worked perfectly well for my use case here with the R extension. What I like most about VS Code is how it gives me one window where I can have everything combined. I can have Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, my Quarto Markdown, and any code that I write. I think it's a great app.

\newpage

# Task 16 --- Favorite AI Data-Viz Tools

- **Claude Code** --- Claude Code is probably by far my most favorite AI tool. I used to exclusively use ChatGPT, but once I made the switch to Claude it opened an entirely new world for me. Claude does a great job at following instructions, and it worked well during this task as well. What I like about Claude as well is the ability to use a CLAUDE.md and give it instructions on how to work properly. I made a very extensive CLAUDE.md to set the guardrails and the requirements for this course, in order to make sure the outputs are as good as possible on their first version. I still had to iterate a lot throughout, but I feel like it would have been worse had I used a different agentic model.
- **Playwright MCP** --- The Playwright MCP was very important for the interactive visualization. It was a game changer, as it allowed Claude to actually review its output, test the interactive visualization itself, and see whether its code worked the way it had intended and whether things actually worked --- instead of me having to test them myself and then give it feedback in this back-and-forth loop. This way Claude could check its own work. This unfortunately didn't mean that the first iteration was already perfect. This was probably the task that took the most time, but I feel like if I hadn't had the Playwright tool, this task would have been a nightmare.
- **GitHub MCP** --- I like this tool a lot because it allows Claude to interact with my GitHub itself. This was crucial in this case for my interactive chart, as that is running over my GitHub, and it allowed Claude to push things to my GitHub and that way work as autonomously as possible with as little input from me. I like this tool a lot in general because it was also very useful for my other classes, but I won't go into that here.
- **Context7 MCP** --- I like this one because it ensures Claude has access to the most recent libraries and changes to code, so it doesn't use any outdated code and is always up to date. This is nothing crazy, but I feel like its usefulness is self-explanatory.
- **Superwhisper** --- I like this one a lot as well because it allowed me to give voice commands to Claude, which made the process of giving feedback and iterating a lot easier. This way I could just talk to Claude and tell it what I wanted, instead of having to write everything down. This was especially useful for the interactive visualization, where I had to give a lot of feedback on how things should work and how they should look, and it was just easier to talk to Claude about it instead of writing everything down.

\newpage

# Task 17 --- Favorite Inspiration Resources

**Data sources**

- **FRED** (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) --- This one is probably one of my favorite datasets, especially because I use it with an API key, which is something I learned in my programming course that I took this semester. And the process of using an API key has something satisfying to it that I enjoy a lot. FRED also has great data, economic data on the US, which is something that's always interesting.
- **USGS** --- What I like about the USGS is that they have a lot of different data on a lot of different topics. They have data on earthquakes, on minerals, on all kinds of things. So it's a great resource to find data on a lot of different topics. The data is also of very good quality and very well documented, which is something I really appreciate.
- **SNB data portal** --- I like the SNB portal a lot because it's the Swiss National Bank, and as a Swiss myself and an economics student, I'm obviously interested in that kind of data.

**Inspiration**

- **Financial Times** --- I like the Financial Times a lot. It's probably the news outlet I read the most on a daily basis. I really like their style of visualization and the colors that they use, so that is something I draw inspiration from.
- **The Economist** --- The Economist is obviously the classic, known for their good visualizations and the very distinct colors they use. However, as mentioned above, I do prefer the style of the Financial Times, even though I have to say The Economist does a great job, and I understand why they are known for their visualizations.

\textbf{Task 11.} BAG, \emph{Krankenversicherungsprämien} (opendata.swiss); canton geometry from \texttt{severinlandolt/map-switzerland}. \url{https://opendata.swiss/de/dataset/health-insurance-premiums}\\[0.25em]
\textbf{Task 12.} USGS ANSS Comprehensive Earthquake Catalog via the FDSN event web service (M$\geq$5, 1980--2025); plate boundaries from Bird (2003), PB2002. \url{https://earthquake.usgs.gov/fdsnws/event/1/}\\[0.25em]
\textbf{Task 13.} FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St.\ Louis), series \texttt{T10Y2Y}, \texttt{USREC}, \texttt{DGS10}, \texttt{DGS2}. \url{https://fred.stlouisfed.org/}
}
